title: Where Your Memories Live, and Why They Change Every Time You Remember
description:
Your memories are not stored in one place, and they are not recordings. Follow a memory from the moment it forms to the night your brain replays it, meet the patient who changed neuroscience, see the experiment that switched a memory on with light, and learn why remembering something can quietly rewrite it.

Sources:
- Queensland Brain Institute, Where are memories stored in the brain?: https://qbi.uq.edu.au/memory/where-are-memories-stored
- OpenStax Psychology 2e, Parts of the Brain Involved with Memory: https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-2-parts-of-the-brain-involved-with-memory
- OpenStax Psychology 2e, Problems with Memory: https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-3-problems-with-memory
- MIT News (2012), Conjuring memories artificially: https://news.mit.edu/2012/conjuring-memories-artificially-0322
- NIMH (2025), How the brain creates new memories while maintaining old ones: https://www.nimh.nih.gov/news/science-updates/2025/how-the-brain-creates-new-memories-while-maintaining-old-ones

This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice.

scenes.narration: Think of your favorite childhood memory. It feels like a recording. It is not. Every time you replay it, your brain rebuilds it.
scenes.headline: YOUR MEMORY IS NOT A RECORDING

visual.note: a pile of old childhood photographs

scenes.narration: Your memories are who you are. Your name, your first day of school, the way to your kitchen in the dark, the smell of a grandparent's house. All of it is stored somewhere inside the tissue of your brain. But where, exactly? And how?
scenes.headline: WHERE DO MEMORIES LIVE?

visual.note: a side view illustration of the human brain

scenes.narration: About a century ago, psychologist Karl Lashley set out to find the answer. He trained rats to run a maze, then damaged different parts of their brains, hoping to erase the memory and pinpoint its location. He was searching for what scientists call an engram, the physical trace of a memory.
scenes.headline: THE HUNT FOR THE ENGRAM
scenes.sub: The physical trace of a memory

visual.note: a white lab rat

scenes.narration: He never found it. No matter which spot he damaged, the rats still remembered something. Lashley concluded that memory was not stored in any single spot. He was partly right, and the full answer would take another century of work.
scenes.headline: HE NEVER FOUND IT

visual.spec: a simple rat maze from above with question marks over several brain regions of a rat silhouette

scenes.narration: Today, neuroscientists know that memories are not kept in one place. Different kinds of memory depend on different, interconnected brain regions. To see how, follow a single memory through its life: how it is made, how it is saved, and what happens every time you bring it back.
scenes.headline: NOT ONE PLACE, MANY

visual.spec: brain outline with several highlighted regions connected by lines: hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum, prefrontal cortex, neocortex

scenes.narration: Say you meet someone new at a party. Your senses take in their face, their voice, the music playing, the room. Each of those details is handled by a different part of your brain. Sight in one area, sound in another, emotion in yet another.
scenes.headline: STEP ONE: MAKING A MEMORY

visual.note: two people shaking hands at a casual party

scenes.narration: Something has to tie those scattered pieces together into a single event. That job falls largely to a curved structure deep in each side of your brain, called the hippocampus. Its name comes from the Greek word for seahorse, because of its shape.
scenes.headline: THE HIPPOCAMPUS

visual.note: the hippocampus highlighted inside the brain

scenes.narration: The hippocampus is crucial for laying down memories of personal events, what scientists call episodic memories. It works like an index in a library. It does not hold every book itself, but it records where the pieces are kept, so they can be found and reassembled later.
scenes.headline: YOUR BRAIN'S INDEX

visual.note: an old wooden library card catalog

scenes.narration: How do we know this? Largely because of one man. His name was Henry Molaison, and for decades, scientists knew him only by his initials, H. M. He may be the most important patient in the history of memory research.
scenes.headline: THE PATIENT KNOWN AS H.M.

visual.query: vintage hospital corridor black and white
visual.note: a vintage hospital corridor in black and white

scenes.narration: In nineteen fifty three, to treat severe epilepsy, surgeons removed tissue from both sides of his brain, including much of the hippocampus. Afterward, he could hold on to new personal memories for only minutes. People he met would be strangers again the next time he saw them.
scenes.headline: MEMORIES THAT LASTED MINUTES

visual.spec: brain seen from below with the hippocampus regions on both sides shaded to show the tissue removed

scenes.narration: Yet much of his older past remained. And when researchers taught him new motor tasks, he got better with practice, even though he could not remember ever practicing. His hands were learning while his conscious memory was not.
scenes.headline: HIS HANDS REMEMBERED

visual.note: a hand carefully tracing a star shape with a pencil

scenes.narration: That revealed two huge truths. First, the hippocampus helps form new memories, but it is not where they are permanently stored. Second, you do not have one memory system. You have several, and they can work independently.
scenes.headline: MORE THAN ONE MEMORY

visual.spec: three labeled branches from one word Memory: explicit for facts and events, implicit for skills and habits, working for short-term holding

scenes.narration: Explicit memories, the facts and events you can consciously recall, rely on the hippocampus, the outer layer of the brain called the neocortex, and the amygdala. Implicit memories, like riding a bike or typing, rely on the basal ganglia and the cerebellum, at the back of your brain.
scenes.headline: FACTS VERSUS SKILLS

visual.note: a child learning to ride a bicycle

scenes.narration: Then there is working memory, the mental notepad you use to hold a phone number for a few seconds. It depends mainly on the prefrontal cortex, just behind your forehead. And the amygdala adds something else to the mix: emotional weight, especially for frightening experiences.
scenes.headline: THE MENTAL NOTEPAD

visual.note: the front of the brain highlighted

scenes.narration: So memories are spread across networks of brain cells. But that left Lashley's old question hanging. Is there a physical engram? Could scientists ever point to a specific set of cells and say, this is a memory? In two thousand twelve, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology did exactly that.
scenes.headline: POINTING TO A MEMORY

visual.note: glowing neurons under a microscope

scenes.narration: Working with mice, neuroscientist Susumu Tonegawa and his colleagues used a technique called optogenetics. They added a light-sensitive protein only to the cells in the hippocampus that were active while a mouse formed a particular memory. In this case, a memory of getting a mild shock in one specific place.
scenes.headline: TAGGING A MEMORY WITH LIGHT

visual.query: laboratory mouse in researcher's gloved hands
visual.note: a lab mouse held gently in gloved hands

scenes.narration: Later, they put the mouse somewhere completely different and simply shone light on those tagged cells. The mouse froze in a defensive crouch, as if it were back where the shock happened. No shock was given. Switching on a small group of cells was enough to bring the memory back.
scenes.headline: A MEMORY SWITCHED ON

visual.spec: a mouse in a new box with a beam of light reaching a small cluster of highlighted neurons, and the mouse shown frozen in place

scenes.narration: As one of the researchers put it, memories really do reside in very specific brain cells. Nearly a century after Lashley began searching, the engram had finally been caught in the act.
scenes.headline: THE ENGRAM, FOUND

visual.note: microscope image of hippocampal neurons

scenes.narration: Now back to your new acquaintance from the party. You have made the memory. But a fresh memory is fragile. To last, it has to be strengthened and woven into what you already know. And much of that work happens when you are not paying attention at all.
scenes.headline: STEP TWO: SAVING IT

visual.query: person falling asleep reading book in bed
visual.note: a person dozing off with a book in bed

scenes.narration: It happens while you sleep. A study funded by the National Institutes of Health found that new memories are reactivated during sleep for several days after they form. The brain replays them again and again, especially during non-REM sleep, which is when memories are consolidated.
scenes.headline: REPLAYED WHILE YOU SLEEP

visual.spec: a sleeping person with a looping replay arrow over the brain and a small calendar showing the replay repeating over several nights

scenes.narration: There is a clever twist. In mice, cells holding older memories and cells holding newer ones tended to replay at different moments of sleep. When researchers disrupted the moments tied to new memories, the mice failed to retain what they had just learned.
scenes.headline: OLD AND NEW TAKE TURNS

visual.note: a small mouse curled up asleep

scenes.narration: Sleep may also clear space. At the University of Wisconsin, researchers measured the connections between brain cells, called synapses, in mice. After sleep, most synapses had shrunk by about eighteen percent. But the largest synapses, which may hold well-established memories, did not shrink.
scenes.headline: SLEEP MAKES ROOM

visual.note: electron microscope image of synapses between neurons

scenes.narration: Think of it like editing a draft overnight. The noise of the day gets trimmed back, the important parts are kept, and your brain wakes up ready to learn again. The lead researcher suspects the same kind of resetting happens in people.
scenes.headline: EDITING THE DRAFT

visual.note: a printed draft being edited with a pen

scenes.narration: So your memory is made, indexed and saved. Here is where the story takes a turn most people never expect. The moment you remember something is also the moment it is most open to change.
scenes.headline: STEP THREE: REMEMBERING

visual.query: person looking at old photograph nostalgic
visual.note: a person holding and studying an old photograph

scenes.narration: Psychologists call it reconstruction. When you recall a memory, your brain does not press play on a stored file. It rebuilds the event from its scattered pieces, filling gaps with what seems likely. And each time, small errors can slip in.
scenes.headline: MEMORY IS REBUILT

visual.spec: puzzle pieces labeled sight, sound, emotion, place being reassembled into a picture, with one piece slightly different from the original

scenes.narration: In a classic experiment from nineteen seventy four, psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people a film of a car crash. Then they asked how fast the cars were going when they hit each other. But they changed one word in the question.
scenes.headline: ONE WORD CHANGES EVERYTHING

visual.note: two toy cars bumping into each other, playful and not graphic

scenes.narration: People who heard the word smashed estimated much higher speeds than people who heard the word contacted. A week later, the smashed group was more than twice as likely to remember seeing broken glass. There was no broken glass in the film.
scenes.headline: GLASS THAT WAS NEVER THERE

visual.spec: two speech bubbles, one saying smashed and one saying contacted, each pointing to a speedometer, the smashed one reading higher

scenes.narration: This is called the misinformation effect. After you are exposed to new and possibly inaccurate information, you may misremember the original event. And it matters far beyond the lab. Mistaken eyewitness identification was a factor in about three quarters of the first two hundred thirty nine wrongful convictions overturned by DNA evidence.
scenes.headline: THE MISINFORMATION EFFECT

visual.note: an empty courtroom with the witness stand

scenes.narration: Even your most vivid memories are not safe. Psychologists call them flashbulb memories, intensely detailed recollections of emotional events. A decade after the September eleventh attacks, ninety seven percent of Americans who were at least eight at the time said they could recall how they heard the news.
scenes.headline: FLASHBULB MEMORIES

visual.note: an old television set in a quiet living room

scenes.narration: Yet research shows these memories can drift over time, just like ordinary ones. They feel just as certain, sometimes even more certain, but the details can quietly change. Confidence and accuracy are not the same thing.
scenes.headline: CONFIDENT, BUT WRONG

visual.note: a soft, out-of-focus photograph suggesting a fading memory

scenes.narration: That might sound unsettling, but it may also be a feature, not a bug. A memory that can be updated lets you fold in new information, connect old experiences to new ones, and imagine the future using pieces of the past.
scenes.headline: A FEATURE, NOT A BUG

visual.query: person looking at city skyline thinking future
visual.note: a person gazing out at a city skyline

scenes.narration: So where do your memories live? Not in one place. They are patterns spread across networks of brain cells, indexed by the hippocampus, colored by the amygdala, polished while you sleep, and rebuilt every single time you call them up.
scenes.headline: PATTERNS, NOT FILES

visual.note: colorful map of the brain's neural pathways

scenes.narration: Which means that your favorite childhood memory is not a dusty file in a drawer. It is alive. Every time you return to it, you are not just remembering your past. You are quietly rewriting it.
scenes.headline: YOU ARE REWRITING IT

visual.note: a child running happily along a beach at sunset

scenes.narration: Follow Inside Your Body for more of the science of you.
